https://www.dw.com/en/trump-grants-visa-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Oupf Prefer DW on Google Zohran Mamdani said he spoke with President Donald Trump on Saturday Image: NDZ/STAR MAX/IPx/picture alliance Advertisement New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Saturday that US President Donald Trump had agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a 15-year-old boy who was killed in a Bronx neighborhood earlier this week. Javits Frimpong moved to New York from Ghana last year to be with his father and begin a new life in the US, according to Representative Ritchie Torres, a Democrat from the Bronx. Frimpong was shot in the abdomen on Thursday morning on his way to school and later died in the hospital, according to New York City police. There have been no arrests in the case so far, with police investigating the shooting. Mamdani says he spoke to Trump "I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately," Mamdani posted on X. "The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away," he wrote. "Javits Frimpong's mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person." The killing led to an outpouring of grief in New York, with Torres writing, "Our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him." The White House is yet to comment on the Trump-Mamdani phone call. Teen was bullied in school, father says Thomas Frimpong remembered his son as a quiet boy and said he was bullied in school by two boys. Ghana's foreign minister, Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa, thanked Mamdani and Trump in a post on X. He said Ghanaian officials were coordinating with Javits Frimpong's mother to assist her with the visa application process. https://www.politico.eu/article/russian-.text: A Russian citizen was charged with espionage in Poland after he was caught taking photographs of the country’s railway infrastructure, police in Lower Silesia said Friday. Authorities said officers patrolling after a football match in Świdnica, south-western Poland, stumbled upon the 55-year-old Russian national as he was taking photographs of passing trains at an unguarded railway crossing. “Everything indicates that the photos he took could be used against the security of the state,” the regional police authority wrote in a press release . Advertisement Advertisement Police found a large amount of evidence suggesting that the man took pictures of strategic infrastructure systematically. “There were photographs of various places and important communication facilities, not only in Poland,” Łukasz Dutkowiak, a spokesperson for the Lower Silesian police, told Radio Wrocław . Prosecutors are now investigating “activities for foreign intelligence against the Republic of Poland,” the regional authority added. Poland has faced multiple sabotage attacks against its military and railway infrastructure over the past year. Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Ukrainian nationals of “cooperating with Russian services” after a November 2025 attack damaged a rail line close to the Polish-Ukrainian border. Fires broke out at a drone-components plant in Skarżysko-Kamienna and an aircraft-parts facility in Lublin in late August. In September, a Starlink communications station was set on fire near Warsaw. “Russia does not even have to cross our border,” Tusk said after the September attacks . “It is already waging a hybrid war against us using drones, acts of sabotage and disinformation on the internet.” European officials have pointed to an escalation of sabotage attacks from Russia over the past few months, as President Vladimir Putin seeks to disrupt military support for Ukraine and raise the political cost of backing Kyiv.
